title: Shurpanakha at the hut
hookLine: a visitor walks up to the hut at Panchavati and tells Rama to leave his wife for her
carry: eka-patni-vrata: rama's vow of one wife
tomorrow: The wound that starts a war

lines: WHO ARE YOU, WITH A BOW?
cards: The quiet ends the way a lot of trouble starts: with someone noticing someone.
Rama sits outside the hut, talking with Sita and Lakshmana, when a rakshasi, a woman of the rakshasa people, comes through the trees and sees him. She stops. She wants him, right then, completely.
She walks straight up and asks: who are you, dressed like a hermit but carrying a bow, with a wife beside you, in a forest that belongs to rakshasas?

teach.h: I AM SHURPANAKHA. BE MY HUSBAND.
teach.b: Rama answers plainly: his name, his father's, Sita's and Lakshmana's, and why they're in the forest. Then he asks who she is.
I am Shurpanakha, she says, sister of Ravana, king of the rakshasas, and of Khara and Dushana, who rule this part of the forest. I saw you and I want you. Be my husband.
Leave this woman. Then it turns ugly: she says she'll eat Sita, and Lakshmana too. Her name means she of the nails like winnowing fans.
Rama's first answer is simple: I'm married, and my wife is here. Then he laughs and suggests she try his brother, and Lakshmana jokes back.
Some readers are uneasy with that teasing; others read it as turning aside a dangerous moment without violence. The text doesn't settle it. But hold on to Rama's first answer, because Hindus have.
Rama's own father had three chief queens. Rama keeps one.
Tradition calls him eka-patni-vrata, the one vowed to a single wife.

teach.h: A GOLDEN IMAGE, NOT A NEW WIFE.
teach.b: Years later in the Ramayana, when a great ritual needs his wife beside him and Sita isn't there, he sets a golden image of her in her place rather than marry again. Here's the teaching under it.

Hinduism doesn't call desire bad. Kama, desire and love, is one of the four aims of a good life, beside dharma, artha and moksha. But kama is meant to run inside dharma, like a river inside its banks.
Shurpanakha is desire with no banks: I want you, so leave her.

teach.h: EKA-PATNI-VRATA: DESIRE KEPT BY A VOW.
teach.b: Rama is desire kept by a vow. That's why many Hindu elders bless a new couple to be like Rama and Sita.

how: Many Hindu elders bless a newly married couple to be like Rama and Sita, and Rama's title eka-patni-vrata, vowed to one wife, is part of why; modern writers have also retold this scene from Shurpanakha's side.

only after that does he joke and send her to Lakshmana.

games.q: someone powerful tells a married man: leave your wife, i'm better. by Rama's example, what fits?
o: say it plainly: i'm married, and my wife is here.
keep it vague, so nobody gets angry.
think it over; his own father had three chief queens.
games.why: Rama's first word is the plain truth: i'm married. tradition calls him eka-patni-vrata, vowed to one wife, though his father had three chief queens.

practice: If there's a picture of Rama and Sita in your home, or a photo of two people you love who kept their promise to each other, look at it for this sit. Notice what held them together: the love, and the vow around it. Breathe slowly.
If nothing like that is near, picture a couple you admire and silently wish them well.

wordCard.voice: Shurpanakha. Ravana's sister, she of the nails like winnowing fans, who sees Rama and demands he marry her.

orig.note: Sanskrit śūrpaṇakhā: śūrpa (winnowing basket) + nakha (nail): she of the nails like winnowing fans.

carryVoice: Hold on to it: eka-patni-vrata, Rama's vow of one wife, desire kept inside dharma. Tomorrow, the jokes run out. That's day five hundred sixty-one.
